Tighten to high-intent keywords and audiences, layer in a real negatives list to cut the tyre-kickers, and stop letting the platform optimise for clicks — make it optimise for purchases or add-to-carts. an0756.user: IELTS prep, running Amazon Ads. Pasting what I've got: this week vs last week my ROAS dropped 22%. That's a big move. I had 66 conversions this week. I'm about to tear up the whole strategy and rebuild the campaigns. What's wrong??
an0756.assistant:
Don't tear up anything. There's nothing to fix here yet.

A 22% ROAS swing on 66 conversions is not a trend — it's noise. With a sample that small, a handful of orders landing on Monday instead of Sunday moves the percentage by exactly this much. You're looking at the random week-to-week jitter every account has, and reading it as a signal.

This is the single most expensive habit a founder can build: reacting to one noisy week, overhauling everything, then the metric reverts on its own and you've thrown away your learnings and reset the algorithm for nothing. That whipsaw costs more than any bad week ever does.

What would actually count as a real shift: the same direction for 3-4 weeks running, or a swing big enough that random noise can't explain it. Until then, the correct action is to do nothing and let it run. Check again in three weeks — if ROAS is still down then, we diagnose. Right now there's no patient to treat.

an0765.user: D2C skincare, post-iOS world and my dashboards are gaslighting me. Meta says my ROAS on this spend is 4.4. Shopify last-click says 1.7 on the same ₹19.5L. They don't match and I genuinely can't tell which one is real. Which dashboard do I trust?
an0765.assistant:
Neither. That's the answer, and it's not a dodge — both dashboards are structurally biased and the truth sits between them.

Meta's 4.4 is inflated: post-iOS it's reporting modelled conversions on a 7-day-click (often plus view-through) window, and it's incentivised to claim credit for every sale it plausibly touched. Shopify last-click at 1.7 is the opposite bias — it hands all the credit to whoever the customer clicked last, so a Meta ad that genuinely sparked the purchase gets zero if the person later arrived via a Google search of your brand name. One over-counts, one under-counts. You're refereeing two scorekeepers who will never agree, and there's no winner to find.

Stop trying. The lever is to anchor on a number neither dashboard can fudge: blended CAC. Total spend ÷ actual new customers from Shopify. On ₹19.5L, divide by the count of genuinely new customers that period and you get a true, all-in cost to acquire — then manage to that, plus your contribution margin, and ignore the platform ROAS theatre.

Caveat: blended CAC needs clean new-vs-returning tagging in Shopify, and it blurs which channel did the work — fine when Meta is your dominant spend, but if you scale a second channel you'll want a holdout/geo test or post-purchase 'how did you hear about us' survey to re-split credit. For now, blended is the honest north star.
